title: SMSF loans to other funds questionable
full_text:
An SMSF can provide a secured loan to another fund to use with a limited recourse borrowing arrangement (LRBA), but both funds need to satisfactorily answer a range of questions to ensure it is legitimate, a sector specialist educator has observed.
Heffron SMSF education specialist Natasha Panagis said the question around this type of lending arrangement was not whether it can be done, but rather should the trustees of each fund do it.
“From a technical perspective, an SMSF can provide a secured loan to a related SMSF that is acquiring an asset under an LRBA. There’s no problem with that, but there are a range of Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act and regulation issues that need to be worked through,” Panagis said during a recent briefing by her firm.
“The first one is the sole purpose test and trustees need to be satisfied that making the loan is genuinely being done to benefit the members of the lending SMSF and their beneficiaries. If the arrangement is primarily helping the members of the borrowing SMSF, that would raise some concerns.”
She added the fund’s trust deed and governing rules must allow the SMSF to act as a lender and the loan has to be consistent with its investment strategy, but was still likely to be blocked by the in-house asset rules.
“In many cases, a loan to a related party is going to count towards the 5 per cent in-house asset limit and this alone is going to prevent the arrangement from being viable,” she said.
“The loan must also be on arm’s-length terms. This is a no-brainer.
“It’s simply not enough to document those arm’s-length terms. You need to comply with them in practice.
“I would also be cautious where the SMSF becomes the lender of last resort. If a commercial lender wouldn’t provide the finance, trustees should ask themselves why is the fund comfortable in taking that risk.”
She pointed out if these issues could be positively addressed by the lending fund, additional questions still had to be considered by the borrowing fund.
“Why borrow from a related SMSF at all? All of the trustees need to be comfortable the arrangement satisfies the sole purpose test and is genuinely being entered into for the benefit of the members of the borrowing fund,” she noted.
“This all ties into the trustee covenants as well, particularly the requirement to act in the best financial interests of the members and the beneficiaries.
“They need to be able to demonstrate the related-party loan is commercially justifiable and it represents a reasonable course of action for the fund.
“If the SMSF could have obtained LRBA finance from another lender on more favourable terms, questions may arise about how entering into a related-party loan satisfies both the sole purpose test and the best financial interest obligations.”
